phys_1_3 G6.issue: The KICD key inquiry question 'Why is the lid of a sufuria made wider?' was missing from the sequence; it is now raised in Lesson 5 and answered at the end. KICD lists this as a key inquiry question but no lesson used it. The expected answer is my physics reasoning, not taken from a KICD teacher's guide: the teacher must confirm the answer they want learners to give. CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL We will return to those in our final lesson when we build our complete explanation. Now return to the parked KICD question: Why is the lid of a sufuria made wider? Expected answer: when the sufuria is heated its metal expands and the pot gets wider, so a lid made slightly wider than the pot sits on the rim and does not drop in or jam; the lid also warms and expands in the steam. Accept any answer that links the lid width to expansion on heating.

phys_1_3 G7.issue: KICD asks learners to meet more ways of measuring temperature (thermocouples, RTDs, thermistors, infrared, silicon diodes) and to search media for information; a short homework task now covers this and the Citizenship and Digital literacy competencies. The lessons only used three thermometers (liquid-in-glass, clinical, bimetallic strip), so the KICD outcome 'measure temperature using different technologies' and its digital-search activity were not covered. Lesson 2 is already full, so this is set as homework; the teacher decides whether to make it a class activity or drop it if learners have no internet access. CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL referencing the cross-section diagram from Lesson 1. KICD EXTENSION (homework): show a digital or infrared thermometer if one is available (many clinics use infrared forehead thermometers). Learners search print or digital media for how one more device measures temperature (thermocouple, resistance thermometer such as an RTD or thermistor, infrared sensor or silicon-diode sensor), write two sentences on its working and record where they found the information.

phys_1_3 G15.issue: Station C: a brass–iron strip bends far more visibly over a candle than brass–copper, so the demonstration uses brass–iron. Brass (about 19 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) and copper (about 17 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) differ by only 2 units, so the bend is hardly visible; brass and iron (about 12 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) differ by 7, about 3.5 times more. Brass-iron is also the usual school kit. The teacher decides which strip their school actually has; if only brass-copper is available, expect only a slight bend. CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL (for a brass–iron strip, the strip bends toward the iron side, so the brass on the outside of the curve expands more)

phys_1_3-103.issue: A calliper opens to about 15 to 20 cm, and the planned 0.1 mm precision is not possible for a 50 cm rod. Flame heating makes the rod temperature (and so ΔT and α) unreliable; steam is the common school method. The teacher must decide what apparatus their school actually has. CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL If apparatus is limited, the teacher conducts the demonstration at the front while all groups record data simultaneously from the projected dial gauge reading. Equipment notes: a vernier calliper cannot measure a 50 cm rod to 0.1 mm, so measure L₀ with a metre rule to the nearest millimetre. A Bunsen flame heats the rod unevenly and a thermometer cannot show the rod's true temperature; if you have a steam generator or a boiling-water can, heat the rod with steam (about 100 °C, so ΔT is known) and measure the lengthening with a dial gauge or a pointer on a scale.

phys_1_3 G16.issue: Added language and access supports: a Kiswahili word list, oral or diagram options for learners who find writing hard. The sequence had no Kiswahili or English-learner supports and few ways to show understanding other than writing. The Kiswahili terms are my suggestion and I cannot verify them; a Kiswahili-teaching colleague must confirm the words and add local alternatives. CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL Write 'ANOMALOUS EXPANSION OF WATER' on the DQB anchor strip. LANGUAGE SUPPORT: start a class word list beside the Driving Question Board with Kiswahili terms such as joto (heat/hotness), halijoto (temperature), kipimajoto (thermometer), barafu (ice), kupanuka (to expand), kusinyaa (to shrink). Let learners explain their ideas first in Kiswahili or a mix of languages, then restate in English using the sentence frames.

USE BRIDGE EXPANSION JOINTS AS THE MAIN LOCAL APPLICATION, AND INCLUDE A RAILWAY EXAMPLE ONLY AFTER CONFIRMATION FROM KENYA RAILWAYS OR A QUALIFIED ENGINEER. phys_1_3-045.issue: Lessons 3, 5 and 6, the supporting phenomena and the Final Explanation say gaps are left between SGR rail sections and that the Thika Superhighway has expansion joints cut into its concrete road surface. Modern standard-gauge track is normally built from long continuously welded rail (expansion is handled by rail stress and anchoring, with joints mainly at bridges and switches) and the Thika Superhighway is largely asphalt with joints on its concrete bridges and flyovers. I could not verify this locally. Please check with an engineer or Kenya Railways; if confirmed, use the older metre-gauge Nairobi-Mombasa line (jointed rails) or a bridge expansion joint instead. The calculations stay the same. CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL No text was changed. The suggestion, if any, is in the issue text above.
